subtopic_detail: switching opioid route and drug when oral morphine causes intolerable toxicity in a patient whose renal function is falling
stem:
You are the palliative care registrar reviewing a 71-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and painful bone disease in the sacrum and femur. He has been taking slow release oral morphine twice daily with immediate release breakthrough doses, and his pain had been well controlled for two months.

Over the past four days his family report that he twitches at rest, plucks at the bedclothes, and sees a cat at the end of the bed that is not there. He is more drowsy but rousable and his pain score has actually risen from three to seven. His creatinine has risen from 92 to 214 micromol/L (60-110) with a urea of 18 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73m2. His calcium corrected for albumin is 2.38 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), sodium and glucose are within normal limits, and he is not febrile. He takes no anticholinergic medication and has had no change in his other drugs.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, multifocal myoclonus at rest, visual hallucinations reported, pupils 2 mm and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 214 micromol/L (60-110) up from 92, urea 18 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73m2, corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.15-2.60)
data_table.Medications: Slow release oral morphine twice daily with immediate release breakthrough, docusate and senna, no anticholinergics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his analgesia?

options.text: Rotate to subcutaneous hydromorphone at a reduced equianalgesic dose and give intravenous fluids
options.rationale: Myoclonus, hyperalgesia and hallucinations with worsening pain despite an unchanged dose are opioid neurotoxicity from accumulating morphine metabolites, which are renally cleared and rise as filtration falls. Rotation to hydromorphone, which has a less problematic metabolite profile, at a dose reduced for incomplete cross-tolerance, together with rehydration, is the standard correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Increase the slow release morphine by fifty per cent because his reported pain score has risen
options.rationale: Treating the rising pain score with more of the same opioid is the trap this presentation is built around, because the hyperalgesia is caused by the metabolite rather than by undertreated disease. Escalation deepens the neurotoxicity and the pain worsens further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Add regular oral haloperidol for the hallucinations and continue the morphine at its present dose
options.rationale: Antipsychotic treats a symptom while leaving the accumulating metabolite in place, so the myoclonus and hyperalgesia continue and sedation deepens. Haloperidol is appropriate for delirium from other causes once the opioid has been corrected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Give intravenous naloxone in titrated doses to reverse the sedation and continue the current regimen
options.rationale: Naloxone is reserved for life threatening respiratory depression, and here the respiratory rate is normal and the pupils are not pinpoint. Reversal would precipitate uncontrolled bone pain and withdrawal without addressing metabolite accumulation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Opioid Analgesics)

options.text: Stop all opioid and manage his bone pain with regular paracetamol and a non-steroidal agent
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of a long standing opioid produces withdrawal and leaves severe metastatic bone pain untreated, and a non-steroidal agent is poorly advised at an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24. The near pair is mild bone pain in a patient with preserved renal function, where a non-steroidal agent is genuinely useful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Morphine is metabolised to morphine-6-glucuronide and morphine-3-glucuronide, both cleared by the kidney, and both accumulate rapidly when filtration falls. The 3-glucuronide is the neuroexcitatory one and produces the recognisable syndrome of multifocal myoclonus, hallucinations, worsening drowsiness and paradoxically rising pain. The correct response is opioid rotation to an agent with a friendlier metabolite profile at a dose reduced for incomplete cross-tolerance, plus rehydration to improve clearance. Escalating the same opioid because the pain score rose is the error that turns a reversible problem into a spiral.
key_points: Rising pain with myoclonus and hallucinations on stable morphine is neurotoxicity, not undertreated pain
Morphine glucuronide metabolites are renally cleared and accumulate as filtration falls
Rotate opioid and reduce the equianalgesic dose for incomplete cross-tolerance
Naloxone is for respiratory depression, not for opioid induced delirium
Non-steroidal agents are poorly suited to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 mL/min/1.73m2
explanation.pearls: When rotating between opioids for toxicity rather than for convenience, reduce the calculated equianalgesic dose by 25 to 50 per cent and cover the gap with breakthrough doses, because published conversion ratios assume full cross-tolerance that does not exist. Fentanyl and buprenorphine have no clinically significant renally cleared active metabolites and are the preferred agents once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2.

subtopic_detail: distinguishing two antibody mediated causes of proximal weakness when the reflex pattern and the response to exertion disagree with the usual teaching
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar assessing a 64-year-old man referred with four months of difficulty rising from a low chair and climbing the stairs at his farm gate. He has smoked thirty cigarettes daily since his twenties and has lost 6 kg without trying.

He describes a dry mouth that has made him carry water everywhere, and erectile difficulty that started around the same time as the weakness. He denies double vision, and his speech and swallowing are unaffected. On examination his hip flexors and shoulder abductors are graded four out of five, and his knee reflexes are absent on first testing but become detectable after he holds a sustained quadriceps contraction for fifteen seconds. Strength in the hip flexors is slightly better after brief maximal exertion than at rest. There is no ptosis and no fatigable weakness of eye closure. Creatine kinase, thyroid function and inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Proximal weakness four out of five at hips and shoulders, no ptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, dry oral mucosa
data_table.Reflexes: Knee reflexes absent at rest, detectable after fifteen seconds of sustained contraction
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase, thyroid function and inflammatory markers within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Steroid myopathy from unrecognised exogenous glucocorticoid exposure over recent months
options.rationale: Glucocorticoid myopathy gives painless proximal weakness with a normal creatine kinase, which fits superficially, but he is on no such medication and it explains neither the autonomic features nor the reflex facilitation. It also spares reflexes entirely. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Corticosteroids)

options.text: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome associated with an underlying small cell lung carcinoma
options.rationale: Post-exercise facilitation of absent reflexes, proximal weakness that improves briefly with exertion, and autonomic features such as dry mouth and erectile dysfunction are the defining triad, and the antibody targets the presynaptic voltage gated calcium channel. In a heavy smoker with weight loss the syndrome is paraneoplastic until the chest is cleared. (Source: Brain Foundation Australia: Neuromuscular Disorders)

options.text: Generalised myasthenia gravis with antibodies to the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor
options.rationale: Myasthenia gravis weakens with sustained activity rather than improving, preserves reflexes, and almost always involves the ocular or bulbar muscles at some point in the illness. The distinguishing relationship is presynaptic calcium channel versus postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor, which is why facilitation occurs in one and fatigue in the other. (Source: Brain Foundation Australia: Neuromuscular Disorders)

options.text: Polymyositis with symmetrical proximal inflammatory muscle involvement of the limb girdles
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy raises creatine kinase in almost all cases and produces no autonomic symptoms and no post-exercise facilitation of reflexes. A normal creatine kinase with these bedside findings effectively excludes it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with proximal and distal involvement
options.rationale: This condition does produce proximal weakness with areflexia, but the areflexia is fixed rather than reversible with contraction, and sensory loss with distal involvement is expected. Autonomic dryness is not a feature. (Source: Brain Foundation Australia: Neuromuscular Disorders)

explanation.summary: Proximal weakness with absent reflexes that reappear after sustained contraction is post-exercise facilitation, and it is close to specific for a presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Antibodies against the voltage gated calcium channel reduce calcium entry and acetylcholine release, and repetitive activity transiently overcomes the block, which is why strength and reflexes briefly improve. Autonomic involvement producing dry mouth and erectile dysfunction reflects the same channel in autonomic ganglia and is not seen in myasthenia gravis. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, overwhelmingly small cell lung carcinoma, so a smoker with weight loss needs chest imaging urgently.
key_points: Post-exercise facilitation of reflexes points to a presynaptic rather than postsynaptic defect
Autonomic features such as dry mouth and impotence separate this syndrome from myasthenia gravis
Ocular and bulbar onset is typical of myasthenia gravis and uncommon here
A normal creatine kinase argues against an inflammatory myopathy
Roughly half of cases are paraneoplastic and small cell lung carcinoma dominates
explanation.pearls: On repetitive nerve stimulation, look for an increment of more than 60 per cent in compound muscle action potential amplitude immediately after ten seconds of maximal voluntary contraction; myasthenia gravis instead shows a decrement of more than 10 per cent at low frequency stimulation. If the initial computed tomography of the chest is clear in a smoker, repeat imaging every three to six months for two years, because the neurological syndrome commonly precedes a detectable tumour.

subtopic_detail: choosing first symptomatic therapy for newly diagnosed parkinsonism in an older patient whose occupation depends on fine motor control
stem:
You are the general physician in a movement disorder clinic. A 74-year-old retired watchmaker who still repairs clocks for a local dealer describes eighteen months of a right hand tremor that is worst when the hand rests in his lap and settles when he reaches for a tool. His wife says his handwriting has shrunk and he no longer swings his right arm when walking.

On examination there is a four hertz rest tremor of the right hand, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist that increases when he taps his left hand, and decrement in amplitude on repetitive finger tapping. His gait is slightly stooped with reduced right arm swing and normal stride length. There is no early postural instability, no vertical gaze restriction, no cerebellar sign and no orthostatic drop in blood pressure. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 28 out of 30 and there are no visual hallucinations. He takes no antiemetic and no antipsychotic, and his symptoms now interfere with his repair work.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, no postural blood pressure drop
data_table.Examination: Four hertz right hand rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist with contralateral activation, decrementing finger tapping, reduced right arm swing
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, no hallucinations
data_table.Medications: No antiemetic, antipsychotic or other dopamine blocking drug

lead_in: Which initial symptomatic therapy would you recommend?

options.text: A monoamine oxidase B inhibitor such as rasagiline as monotherapy at the standard daily dose
options.rationale: This class gives a genuine but modest benefit and is a reasonable choice for mild symptoms not yet affecting function. It is unlikely to restore the fine motor precision that his clock repair work demands. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Deferring drug therapy with physiotherapy and review in six months given his preserved gait
options.rationale: Deferring is defensible while symptoms are not interfering with function, but he has told you they now interfere with the work he values. Exercise should accompany drug therapy rather than replace it once function is affected. (Source: Parkinson's Australia: Clinical Information)

options.text: Levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor, titrated slowly from a low starting dose
options.rationale: Levodopa gives the largest and most reliable motor benefit and is the preferred first agent in patients over about seventy, where the neuropsychiatric and impulse control risks of dopamine agonists outweigh their dyskinesia sparing advantage. His symptoms already impair skilled work, which is the trigger to treat rather than observe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: A non-ergot dopamine agonist such as pramipexole, titrated slowly from a low starting dose
options.rationale: Agonists are considered in younger patients to defer motor complications, but in this age group they cause substantially more somnolence, hallucinations, oedema and impulse control disorder for less motor benefit. The distinguishing consideration is age and cognitive reserve rather than tremor severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: An anticholinergic such as benzhexol, titrated slowly from a low starting dose for the tremor
options.rationale: Anticholinergics can help rest tremor but are avoided beyond middle age because of confusion, urinary retention and constipation, and they do nothing for bradykinesia or rigidity. His shrinking handwriting and decrementing finger taps are the disabling features. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antiparkinson Drugs)

explanation.summary: Asymmetric rest tremor with cogwheel rigidity, decrementing repetitive movement and reduced arm swing, in the absence of red flags such as early falls, vertical gaze palsy, cerebellar signs or prominent autonomic failure, is straightforward idiopathic parkinsonism. The decision to treat rests on functional impact, and skilled fine motor work that he can no longer perform meets that bar. In patients over about seventy, levodopa is preferred first line because dopamine agonists carry markedly higher rates of somnolence, hallucination and impulse control disorder with less motor benefit. Anticholinergics are avoided in this age group and address only tremor.
key_points: Treat when symptoms interfere with function, not at an arbitrary disease stage
Levodopa is first line above roughly seventy years of age
Dopamine agonists defer dyskinesia but cause more neuropsychiatric harm in older patients
Anticholinergics treat tremor only and are poorly tolerated beyond middle age
Absent red flags such as early falls or vertical gaze palsy support the idiopathic diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Contralateral activation, asking the patient to tap the opposite hand while you assess wrist tone, unmasks subtle cogwheel rigidity that is undetectable at rest and is the most useful bedside manoeuvre in early disease. Warn every patient starting levodopa that nausea in the first fortnight is managed with domperidone rather than metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, because the latter two cross the blood brain barrier and block the very receptors you are trying to stimulate.

subtopic_detail: sequencing haematinic replacement when macrocytic anaemia is accompanied by posterior column signs and both vitamin levels are low
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman in the assessment unit with three months of tiredness and unsteadiness that is worse in the dark. She has vitiligo and treated hypothyroidism and follows a strict vegan diet begun eleven years ago.

She describes pins and needles in both feet that has crept up to mid-calf. On examination vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at the knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes, and Romberg is positive. Reflexes are brisk at the knees with extensor plantar responses. Her haemoglobin is 96 g/L (115-155) with a mean cell volume of 112 fL (80-100), and the film shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 is 84 pmol/L (150-700) and red cell folate is 220 nmol/L (>360). Thyroid function is within normal limits on her current thyroxine dose and there is no alcohol history.

data_table.Examination: Absent ankle vibration sense, impaired great toe joint position sense, positive Romberg, brisk knee reflexes with extensor plantars
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 112 fL (80-100), hypersegmented neutrophils on film, vitamin B12 84 pmol/L (150-700), red cell folate 220 nmol/L (>360)
data_table.Background: Vegan diet for eleven years, vitiligo, treated hypothyroidism with normal thyroid function

options.text: High dose oral cyanocobalamin now with oral folic acid added after the first week of treatment
options.rationale: High dose oral cobalamin works well through passive absorption for uncomplicated deficiency, including dietary and pernicious causes, but the parenteral route is preferred when neurological signs are present. The distinguishing factor is the cord involvement rather than the underlying cause of the deficiency. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Vitamin B12)

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells now and commence both vitamins once the haemoglobin is safe
options.rationale: A haemoglobin of 96 g/L in a woman who has adapted over months does not meet a transfusion threshold, and transfusion in severe megaloblastic anaemia risks fluid overload for no benefit. The reticulocyte response to cobalamin begins within days. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Patient Blood Management)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Patient Blood Management

options.text: Withhold both vitamins until intrinsic factor antibody and gastroscopy results clarify the cause
options.rationale: Establishing whether there is an autoimmune gastritis matters for lifelong therapy and cancer surveillance, but the samples can be taken now and treatment started the same day. Delaying replacement for investigation risks irreversible cord damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin now with oral folic acid added only after the cobalamin is running
options.rationale: When both are deficient, cobalamin must be replaced first or started simultaneously, because folate alone restores erythropoiesis while allowing the neurological lesion to progress. The parenteral route is chosen because she has neurological involvement, where reliable and rapid repletion matters more than convenience. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Oral folic acid 5 mg daily now with cobalamin added once the blood count has begun to respond
options.rationale: Giving folate first is the classic and genuinely harmful error, because it corrects the megaloblastic anaemia and removes the haematological warning sign while subacute combined degeneration of the cord advances. The cord lesion, not the anaemia, is what determines her long term function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, dorsal column signs and upper motor neurone reflexes is subacute combined degeneration of the cord from cobalamin deficiency. When folate is also low, the sequencing of replacement is the whole exam point: folate given alone drives haematopoiesis using the remaining cobalamin and accelerates neurological deterioration while making the blood count look better. Cobalamin is therefore given first or at the same time, and the parenteral route is preferred whenever neurological features are present. Her vegan diet plus vitiligo and autoimmune thyroid disease means both dietary insufficiency and autoimmune gastritis should be pursued, but investigation never delays treatment.
key_points: Replace cobalamin before or with folate, never folate alone, when both are deficient
Neurological involvement makes the parenteral route preferred over high dose oral therapy
Hypersegmented neutrophils and a mean cell volume above 110 fL point to megaloblastic rather than other macrocytosis
Brisk reflexes with extensor plantars plus dorsal column loss localise to the cord, not a peripheral neuropathy
Vitiligo with autoimmune thyroid disease raises the prior probability of autoimmune gastritis
explanation.pearls: Check potassium two to four days after starting cobalamin, because the burst of erythropoiesis drives potassium into new cells and can produce a clinically significant fall in a patient who was not hypokalaemic at baseline. Neurological recovery correlates with the duration of symptoms before treatment, so deficits present for more than six months frequently leave a permanent residue even with perfect replacement.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Patient Blood Management

subtopic_detail: headache with papilloedema in a young woman on a drug that is itself a recognised precipitant of raised pressure
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman referred by her optometrist. She has had a daily headache for seven weeks that is worse on waking and when she bends forward, and twice this week her vision has greyed out completely for a few seconds when she stood up quickly. She also describes a rhythmic whooshing in her right ear that matches her pulse.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she started oral isotretinoin for acne four months ago. Fundoscopy shows bilateral disc swelling with blurred margins and loss of spontaneous venous pulsation. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye and formal perimetry shows an enlarged blind spot bilaterally with no other field defect. There is no focal neurological deficit and no fever. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with venography is reported as showing no mass lesion, no hydrocephalus and patent dural venous sinuses.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema with absent venous pulsation, visual acuity 6/6 both eyes, no focal deficit, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Perimetry: bilateral enlarged blind spot only
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance brain with venography: no mass, no hydrocephalus, patent dural venous sinuses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start acetazolamide and arrange outpatient neurology review in six weeks without further testing
options.rationale: Acetazolamide is the right drug once the diagnosis is secure, but starting it without a measured opening pressure leaves the diagnosis presumptive and a treatable alternative unexcluded. Normal imaging alone does not confirm raised pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop the isotretinoin and review the discs in three months with repeat visual field testing
options.rationale: Withdrawing the retinoid is an essential part of management because it is a recognised precipitant, but observation over three months risks permanent field loss while the pressure remains untreated. The drug is stopped in parallel with, not instead of, establishing the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Retinoids)

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
options.rationale: Sinus thrombosis is the key structural mimic and must always be excluded, but magnetic resonance venography has already done so and repeating the question with a different modality adds radiation without information. The near pair remains worth remembering because it can present identically with headache, papilloedema and pulsatile tinnitus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for optic nerve sheath fenestration now given the presence of bilateral disc swelling
options.rationale: Surgical decompression is reserved for rapidly progressive visual loss that fails medical therapy, and her acuity is 6/6 with only enlarged blind spots. Operating at this stage exposes her to surgical risk that the visual findings do not justify. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Papilloedema)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Papilloedema

options.text: Lumbar puncture with measurement of the opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid analysis
options.rationale: With imaging that excludes a mass and confirms patent sinuses, the diagnosis of raised intracranial pressure without a structural cause requires a documented elevated opening pressure with normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents. That measurement both establishes the diagnosis and guides how urgently vision must be protected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Daily headache worse on waking and on bending, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus and bilateral papilloedema in a young woman with a raised body mass index describes idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The diagnosis is one of exclusion and requires neuroimaging with venography to rule out a mass and sinus thrombosis, followed by a lumbar puncture documenting a raised opening pressure with normal constituents. Isotretinoin, tetracyclines, excess vitamin A and withdrawal of corticosteroids are recognised precipitants and must be identified and stopped. Acuity is typically preserved until late, so an enlarged blind spot with normal acuity is reassuring but not a reason to defer diagnosis.
key_points: Imaging with venography comes first, then lumbar puncture for opening pressure and constituents
Pulsatile tinnitus with transient visual obscurations is the characteristic symptom pairing
Retinoids, tetracyclines and vitamin A excess are recognised drug precipitants
Normal visual acuity with an enlarged blind spot is the usual early field finding
Surgical decompression is reserved for progressive visual loss despite medical therapy
explanation.pearls: An opening pressure above 25 cmH2O in a non-obese adult, or above 28 cmH2O when measured in a sedated or obese patient, supports the diagnosis provided the fluid constituents are normal. Track the condition with formal perimetry rather than acuity, because central vision is preserved until very late and relying on the Snellen chart is how patients lose peripheral field irreversibly.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Papilloedema

subtopic_detail: separating a delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity from the epidermal detachment syndromes when both a rash and a fever follow a new anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 33-year-old man admitted with fever and a rash. He was started on lamotrigine five weeks ago after a first unprovoked seizure and the dose was escalated over that period.

He has a confluent morbilliform eruption covering about 70 per cent of his body surface with marked facial swelling, particularly periorbital. The rash is not tender, Nikolsky sign is negative, and there are no erosions on the lips, conjunctivae or genitals. His pulse rate is 106 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air and temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius. Bloods show white cells 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 384 units/L (5-40), alkaline phosphatase 180 units/L (30-110), creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110) and atypical lymphocytes on the film. There is bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform rash over 70 per cent body surface, marked periorbital and facial oedema, negative Nikolsky sign, no mucosal erosions, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cells 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 384 units/L (5-40), creatinine 138 micromol/L (60-110), atypical lymphocytes on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start systemic corticosteroid with organ monitoring for at least several weeks
options.rationale: Facial oedema, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis five weeks into a new anticonvulsant define the delayed multiorgan hypersensitivity reaction, which is treated by immediate withdrawal of the culprit and systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper. Prolonged monitoring is required because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and transfer to a burns unit for management of epidermal detachment
options.rationale: The epidermal detachment syndromes are excluded here by a negative Nikolsky sign, absent mucosal erosions and a non-tender rash, and they do not produce eosinophilia or facial oedema. The distinguishing relationship is that one is a delayed eosinophilic multiorgan reaction and the other is keratinocyte apoptosis with skin loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Continue lamotrigine at a reduced dose with antihistamine and emollient for a benign drug rash
options.rationale: A simple morbilliform drug eruption has no fever, no organ involvement and no eosinophilia, and can sometimes be treated through. Organ dysfunction in two systems makes continuing the drug at any dose unsafe. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antiepileptics)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start intravenous immunoglobulin as the primary immunomodulatory therapy
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has been used in severe epidermal detachment and in refractory cases, but it is not the first line immunomodulator for this syndrome and the evidence for it here is weak. Corticosteroid remains the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and treat empirically for acute Epstein-Barr virus infection with supportive care
options.rationale: Atypical lymphocytes and lymphadenopathy do suggest a viral illness, and reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 or Epstein-Barr virus genuinely occurs within this syndrome, but that reactivation is part of the reaction rather than an alternative diagnosis. Supportive care alone leaves the hepatitis and renal impairment untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: The combination of a late onset rash two to eight weeks after a new anticonvulsant, facial oedema, fever, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis is the delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity syndrome. It is distinguished from the epidermal detachment syndromes by a negative Nikolsky sign, absent mucosal erosion, a non-tender eruption and the presence of eosinophilia, and from a benign morbilliform eruption by fever and organ involvement. Management is immediate cessation of the culprit drug and systemic corticosteroid with a prolonged taper, because abrupt withdrawal of steroid commonly triggers relapse. Herpesvirus reactivation occurs within the syndrome and is not an alternative explanation.
key_points: Onset two to eight weeks after the drug distinguishes this from an immediate hypersensitivity reaction
Facial oedema with eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes is the recognisable signature
Negative Nikolsky sign and intact mucosae argue against epidermal detachment syndromes
Systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over weeks is first line, not immunoglobulin
Aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides and vancomycin are the usual culprits
explanation.pearls: Recheck thyroid function at three months after recovery, because autoimmune thyroiditis develops in up to a fifth of patients and appears long after the rash has cleared. Label the culprit in the allergy record along with its cross-reacting relatives: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone and lamotrigine cross-react frequently enough that sodium valproate or levetiracetam should be chosen for future seizure control.

subtopic_detail: managing a catecholamine crisis precipitated in a patient already taking a beta blocker before the diagnosis was suspected
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward. A 49-year-old woman admitted yesterday for investigation of episodic palpitations, drenching sweats and headaches was started on metoprolol 50 mg twice daily last night by the covering doctor for a presumed tachyarrhythmia. She had a computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast this morning.

Thirty minutes after returning from the scan she became acutely unwell with a crushing headache, pallor and vomiting. Her pulse rate is 128 per minute, blood pressure 248/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 92 per cent on room air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. She has bibasal crackles and a third heart sound. The scan report describes a 5 cm right adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 38 Hounsfield units and marked heterogeneous enhancement. Her plasma free metanephrines, sent yesterday, have just returned at more than six times the upper limit of normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 per minute, blood pressure 248/142 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 92 per cent room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, bibasal inspiratory crackles, third heart sound, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free metanephrines more than six times the upper limit of normal
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography abdomen: 5 cm right adrenal mass, unenhanced attenuation 38 Hounsfield units, heterogeneous enhancement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.text: Start an intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion alone and withhold any further adrenergic blockade
options.rationale: Nitrate will lower the pressure transiently but does nothing about the receptor level problem, so the pressure oscillates as catecholamine release continues. Leaving the beta blocker in place without alpha cover perpetuates the underlying mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start intravenous phentolamine and continue the beta blocker once alpha blockade is established
options.rationale: Beta blockade given before alpha blockade leaves alpha mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which is what has converted her episodic symptoms into a crisis with pulmonary oedema. The correction is immediate alpha blockade with a short acting intravenous agent, after which beta blockade can safely continue to control the reflex tachycardia. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Increase the metoprolol dose and add intravenous frusemide for the pulmonary congestion present
options.rationale: More beta blockade worsens the unopposed alpha stimulation that is driving the crisis, and the pulmonary oedema here is a consequence of extreme afterload rather than primary fluid overload. This is the specific escalation that has caused deaths in reported cases. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Start intravenous labetalol, relying on its combined alpha and beta receptor blocking activity
options.rationale: Labetalol looks attractive because it blocks both receptors, but its beta to alpha potency ratio is roughly seven to one, so in practice it behaves like a beta blocker in this setting and can worsen the crisis. The distinguishing point is the ratio, not the presence of alpha activity. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Phaeochromocytoma)

options.text: Start oral phenoxybenzamine and arrange surgical resection of the adrenal mass within the week
options.rationale: Oral phenoxybenzamine is the right agent for the elective ten to fourteen day preoperative preparation, but it is too slow for a patient with a systolic pressure of 248 mmHg and pulmonary oedema now. Operating in the middle of an uncontrolled crisis carries a very high mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with a heterogeneous adrenal mass of high unenhanced attenuation and grossly raised metanephrines is a catecholamine secreting tumour. Introducing a beta blocker before alpha blockade removes beta mediated vasodilatation while leaving alpha mediated vasoconstriction intact, and contrast administration can trigger release, which together explain the crisis. Immediate treatment is intravenous alpha blockade with a short acting agent such as phentolamine, with the beta blocker retained once the alpha receptor is covered. Oral phenoxybenzamine and surgery belong to the elective pathway after the crisis is controlled.
key_points: Alpha blockade always precedes beta blockade in catecholamine excess
Beta blockade first leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate crisis
Labetalol is predominantly a beta blocker and is unsuitable as sole therapy here
Unenhanced attenuation above 10 Hounsfield units makes a benign adenoma unlikely
Elective surgery follows ten to fourteen days of oral alpha blockade, never a crisis
explanation.pearls: Prepare elective patients with phenoxybenzamine titrated until a postural drop appears and the haematocrit falls, and liberalise salt and fluid intake in the final days, because the intravascular volume is chronically contracted and collapse after tumour devascularisation is the main intraoperative danger. Any adrenal incidentaloma with unenhanced attenuation above 10 Hounsfield units should have biochemical exclusion of catecholamine excess before any biopsy or procedure is contemplated.

subtopic_detail: deciding on timing of valve surgery when embolic and haemodynamic indications conflict with a very recent cerebral event
stem:
You are the medical registrar on the cardiology ward. A 52-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve has been on intravenous benzylpenicillin for six days for viridans streptococcal endocarditis, and his blood cultures cleared after forty eight hours. He has remained afebrile for four days.

This morning he developed sudden left arm and leg weakness. Computed tomography of the brain performed two hours ago shows a right middle cerebral artery territory infarct of about 2 cm with no haemorrhagic transformation. His pulse rate is 104 per minute, blood pressure 108/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 94 per cent on room air and temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. He has a new early diastolic murmur, bibasal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure. Transoesophageal echocardiography today shows a 16 mm mobile aortic vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation with premature mitral valve closure, and no abscess. His weakness has not progressed and he is fully alert.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 per minute, blood pressure 108/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 94 per cent room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, left hemiparesis four out of five, new early diastolic murmur, bibasal crackles, raised jugular venous pressure
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography brain: 2 cm right middle cerebral artery infarct without haemorrhagic transformation
data_table.Echocardiography: 16 mm mobile aortic vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation with premature mitral valve closure, no abscess

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation about valve surgery?

options.text: Avoid valve surgery altogether and add therapeutic anticoagulation to prevent further embolism
options.rationale: Anticoagulation does not prevent vegetation embolism and substantially raises the risk of haemorrhagic transformation of a fresh infarct. It is continued only where there is an independent indication such as a mechanical prosthesis. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

options.text: Delay valve surgery for seventy two hours and repeat brain imaging to confirm infarct stability
options.rationale: A short delay for repeat imaging is reasonable when the haemodynamics are stable and the neurological picture is uncertain, but this patient has pulmonary congestion with premature mitral valve closure and cannot safely wait. The near pair is the neurologically stable patient with moderate regurgitation, where a brief delay is entirely appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Proceed to valve surgery now, since a non-haemorrhagic small infarct does not require postponement
options.rationale: Severe aortic regurgitation with premature mitral valve closure and pulmonary congestion is a haemodynamic indication for early surgery that outweighs the small ischaemic stroke, and current guidance is that a non-haemorrhagic infarct without extensive damage or coma does not mandate delay. A large mobile vegetation after a first embolic event adds a second indication. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

options.text: Delay valve surgery for four weeks after the stroke to avoid haemorrhagic transformation on bypass
options.rationale: A four week delay applies to haemorrhagic stroke, not to a small bland infarct, and premature mitral valve closure signals acute severe regurgitation that patients do not survive for four weeks. The distinguishing factor is the presence or absence of intracranial blood, not the presence of a stroke as such. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

options.text: Delay valve surgery until the full six week antibiotic course is finished with repeat cultures taken
options.rationale: Completing antibiotics before operating is a common misconception, and surgery is not contraindicated by an incomplete course when a haemodynamic indication exists. Cultures have already cleared, which lowers the risk of prosthetic seeding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Three separate indications for surgery in endocarditis are heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection, and prevention of embolism from a large mobile vegetation, and the first of these is the most urgent. Premature mitral valve closure on echocardiography indicates acute severe aortic regurgitation with left ventricular end diastolic pressure exceeding left atrial pressure, which is a surgical emergency rather than a finding to monitor. A small ischaemic infarct without haemorrhagic transformation, in an alert patient whose deficit is not progressing, does not require surgery to be postponed. Delay of around four weeks applies specifically to intracranial haemorrhage, and completing the antibiotic course first is not required.
key_points: Heart failure from valve destruction is the most urgent surgical indication in endocarditis
Premature mitral valve closure signals acute severe aortic regurgitation and imminent decompensation
A small bland infarct in an alert patient does not mandate postponing surgery
Haemorrhagic stroke, not ischaemic stroke, drives the four week delay
Anticoagulation does not prevent septic embolism and risks haemorrhagic transformation
explanation.pearls: Vegetations larger than 10 mm that have already embolised, and any vegetation larger than 15 mm, justify early surgery for embolic prevention even when the haemodynamics are stable, with most embolic events occurring in the first two weeks of antibiotic therapy. Obtain cerebral imaging in every left sided endocarditis before surgery even without neurological signs, because a clinically silent mycotic aneurysm changes both the timing and the anticoagulation plan.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis

subtopic_detail: responding to a sodium rise that has exceeded the safe daily limit partway through correction of chronic hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old woman admitted eighteen hours ago. She had been drinking heavily for years, eating little, and taking a thiazide started three months ago. Her admission sodium was 104 mmol/L (135-145) with a serum osmolality of 228 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 96 mmol/kg and urine sodium 12 mmol/L. She was confused but had no seizure.

She was given a single 100 mL bolus of hypertonic saline for confusion, the thiazide was ceased, and she then received 1 litre of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent. Over the past few hours her urine output has risen to 380 mL per hour and is dilute. Her sodium is now 121 mmol/L, having risen 17 mmol/L in eighteen hours. She is alert and orientated with no focal neurological deficit, her observations are within normal limits, and her potassium and glucose are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no focal neurological deficit, mucous membranes moist, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Admission sodium 104 mmol/L (135-145), current sodium 121 mmol/L, serum osmolality 228 mmol/kg on admission, urine osmolality 96 mmol/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L
data_table.Fluid balance: Urine output 380 mL per hour and dilute over the past few hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Give a further 100 mL bolus of hypertonic saline because the sodium remains below 125 mmol/L
options.rationale: Hypertonic boluses are for active neurological emergency such as seizure or obtundation, not for a number below an arbitrary line in an alert patient. Further sodium loading here compounds the overcorrection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Restrict fluid to 800 mL daily and recheck the sodium in six hours without other intervention
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the treatment for the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, but her admission biochemistry with dilute urine and a low urine sodium indicates a hypovolaemic and low solute picture instead. Restriction would accelerate the rise rather than slow it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a tolvaptan dose to control the free water handling and recheck the sodium in four hours
options.rationale: Vasopressin receptor antagonists promote free water excretion and would drive the sodium higher still, which is the opposite of what is needed. The near pair is euvolaemic hyponatraemia resistant to restriction, where a short course can be justified under close monitoring. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Tolvaptan)

options.text: Give desmopressin with 5 per cent dextrose to relower the sodium toward the intended daily target
options.rationale: A rise of 17 mmol/L in eighteen hours far exceeds the 8 to 10 mmol/L daily ceiling and places her at real risk of osmotic demyelination, which typically appears days later and is often irreversible. The established rescue is desmopressin to stop the aquaresis together with electrolyte free water, deliberately bringing the sodium back down into the intended range. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Continue the current plan unchanged because she is alert with no neurological deficit at present
options.rationale: Normal neurology now is expected and reassures nobody, because osmotic demyelination characteristically declares itself two to six days after the overcorrection with dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis. Waiting for symptoms means waiting until the injury is done. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Chronic hyponatraemia must be corrected no faster than about 8 to 10 mmol/L in any twenty four hour period, and slower still when risk factors such as alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalaemia or a sodium below 105 mmol/L are present. Removing the cause, here a thiazide and low solute intake, characteristically unleashes a brisk water diuresis once vasopressin is suppressed, and the sodium then overshoots without anyone giving more sodium. The rescue is to stop the aquaresis with desmopressin while replacing electrolyte free water with dextrose, relowering the sodium into the intended range. Normal neurology at the time of overcorrection is the rule rather than the exception, because osmotic demyelination is delayed by days.
key_points: Correction limit is 8 to 10 mmol/L per twenty four hours, and 8 mmol/L in high risk patients
Autocorrection by water diuresis is the usual mechanism of accidental overcorrection
Desmopressin plus 5 per cent dextrose is the standard relowering rescue
Osmotic demyelination presents two to six days later and is frequently irreversible
Dilute urine with low urine sodium separates this picture from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis
explanation.pearls: In a patient with sodium below 110 mmol/L plus alcohol use or malnutrition, consider proactive desmopressin clamping from the outset with hypertonic saline titrated against it, which controls the rate rather than chasing it. Measure sodium every two hours during active correction, because urine output above 200 mL per hour with dilute urine predicts an overshoot several hours before the serum value shows it.
